en: *Samayabhedoparacanacakra-śāstra*, one fascicle.
Composed by the Bodhisattva Vasumitra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when more than a hundred years had passed,
the various schools of the holy teaching arose;
because they brought about mutual harm and clung to divergent views, the various schools emerged one after another.
Relying upon his own Āgama, the great Bodhisattva Vasumitra—
possessing great wisdom, insight, and discernment,
a true Bhikṣu of the Śākya clan— contemplated those tenets and analyzed them with discerning thought.
Equally observing all worlds, which are tossed about by various views and fragmented by the words of the Munis— those respective doctrines shall be explained;
one should carefully examine the Buddha’s teaching and rely upon the proclamation of the Noble Truths.
It is thus heard: after the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha, the Bhagavān, one selects and takes what is real from among the sand, just as if gathering gold.
More than one hundred years had passed since the time of the Sage;
it was as if the sun had long been submerged.
In the city of Kusumapura in the kingdom of Magadha, there reigned a king named Aśoka.
He governed Jambudvīpa and was graced with a single white canopy;
his transformative influence harmonized both humans and spirits.
At that time, the Great Assembly of the Buddha’s Dharma was first divided;
it is said that because the four assemblies disagreed regarding the five points of Mahādeva,
they split into two schools.
First, the Mahāsāṃghika;
second, the Sthavira.
What are the four groups?
First, the assembly of noble elephants;
second, the assembly from the borderlands;
third, the assembly of those who have heard much.
O assembly of the four great virtues,
as for those five matters,
it is as stated in that verse:
Those who are led astray by others and lack knowledge,
who waver and enter the path through the influence of another's voice— this is called the True Buddhist Teaching;
it occurs immediately after this second century.
From within the Mahāsāṃghika school, three sub-sects emerged: first, the Lokottaravāda;
second, the Prajñaptivāda.
Third is the Kukkuṭika school.
Subsequently, during this second century,
another school emerged from within the Mahāsāṃghika.
It was named the Bahuśrutīya school.
Subsequently, during this second century,
another school emerged from within the Mahāsāṃghika.
In the second century after the passing [of the Buddha], during the time when the Prajñaptivāda school was flourishing,
there was a certain renunciant from among the non-Buddhist outsiders.
He abandoned heterodoxy to return to the orthodox path;
he was also named Mahādeva.
He left the household life and received full ordination within the Mahāsāṃghika school.
Being learned and diligent,
he resided at Mount Caitya and,
together with the monks of that school, deliberated once more upon the five matters.
Consequently, due to this schism, they divided into three schools:
first, the Caitīya school;
second, the Aparaśaila school.
Third is the Uttaraśaila school.
Thus, the Mahāsāṃghika school underwent four or five schisms;
when the primary and secondary branches are distinguished, they form nine schools in total.
1. Mahāsāṃghika; 2. Ekavyāvahārika; 3. Lokottaravādin.
4. The Kukkuṭika school;
5. The Bahulika school;
6. The Prajñaptivāda school.
7. The Saptaparvata-vāsin school;
8. The Aparaśaila school;
9. The Uttaraśaila school.
The Sūtras of the Theravāda remained in a state of harmonious unity for that length of time; however,
at the beginning of the third century, a slight dispute arose,
and they were divided into two schools.
First is the Sarvāstivāda,
also known as the Hetuvāda;
second is the Mūlasarvāstivāda.
It was subsequently renamed the Himavat School.
Later, during this very third century,
a school emerged from the Sarvāstivāda.
They are called the Vātsīputrīya school.
Subsequently, during this third century,
four schools branched out from the Vātsīputrīyas.
1. The Ekavyāvahārika school;
2. the Bahuśrutīya school;
3. the Saṃmitīya school.
The fourth is the Gahvaraparvata school.
Subsequently, during this third century,
[it arose] from the Sarvāstivāda school.
Furthermore, another school emerged,
named the Mahīśāsaka.
This occurred subsequently, during this third century.
From the Mahīśāsaka school emerged a branch named the Dharmaguptaka,
which claimed that its lineage had inherited the teachings of the master Śāṇavāsin.
At the end of the third century,
another school emerged from the Sarvāstivāda.
They were called the Kāśyapīya school,
also known as the Sannāgarika school;
this was at the beginning of the fourth century [after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa].
From the Sarvāstivāda school,
another sect emerged,
named the Sautrāntika.
They are also called the Saṃmatīya school.
They claim that they take Ānanda as their teacher.
Thus, the Sthavira school split seven times, or eight times.
When explained by distinguishing between the root and the branches, they form eleven schools: first, the Sarvāstivāda;
second, the Haimavata.
3. The Vatsīputrīya school;
4. The Dharmottarīya school;
5. The Bhadrayānīya school.
6. The Saṃmitīya school;
7. The Mahāśaila school;
8. The Mūlasarvāstivāda school.
9. Dharmaguptaka school;
10. Kāśyapīya school; 11. Sautrāntika school.
I shall now explain the fundamental tenets and derivative tenets, as well as the common and divergent doctrines, of these various schools.
Among these, there are the Mahāsāṃghika,
the Ekavyāvahārika,
and the Lokottaravāda schools.
Regarding the Kukkutika school,
those who hold the same tenets as the fundamental sect are said to be the four schools that teach in common.
All Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have transcended the world.
All Tathāgatas are free from all out-flowing dharmas (*āsrava*).
Every word of the Tathāgatas turns the wheel of the Dharma.
The Buddha expounds all dharmas with a single voice.
Nothing that the World-Honored One speaks does not accord with the truth.
The physical body of the Tathāgata is truly without limit.
The majestic power of the Tathāgata is likewise boundless,
and the lifespan of the Buddhas is also boundless.
The Buddha never tires of transforming sentient beings and causing them to give rise to pure faith.
The Buddha has no sleep or dreams.
The Tathāgata does not require deliberation when answering questions.
At all times, the Buddha does not speak of names and so forth.
Because he is always in meditative concentration, sentient beings,
upon hearing his name and so forth, experience great joy and exultation.
In a single moment of mind, one comprehends all phenomena;
in a single moment of mind associated with wisdom (*prajñā*), one knows all phenomena.
The Tathāgatas, the World-Honored Ones, are constantly accompanied by the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
Up until their final parinirvāṇa,
all bodhisattvas who enter the mother’s womb do not take up the kalala, arbuda, peśī, or ghana as their own physical basis.
When all Bodhisattvas enter their mother’s womb,
they take the form of a white elephant;
when all Bodhisattvas emerge from their mother’s womb, [they likewise do so].
All emerge from the right side.
No bodhisattva gives rise to thoughts of desire, malice, or harm.
It is because the bodhisattva wishes to benefit sentient beings.
May they be able to go to the evil destinies at will;
and by means of the knowledge at the edge of clear realization in a single kṣaṇa,
may they thoroughly know the distinctions between all the characteristics of the four truths.
The five groups of consciousness, beginning with the eye-consciousness, are subject to both defilement and freedom from defilement.
The form and formless realms possess all six groups of consciousness.
The five types of material sense-faculties have as their substance a mass of flesh.
The eye does not see forms;
the ear does not hear sounds;
the nose does not smell fragrances.
The tongue does not taste flavors;
the body does not perceive tangibles;
yet while in the state of meditative equipoise, one utters speech.
There is also the mind of subduing,
and there is also the mental attention of purification;
having accomplished what was to be done, there is no further room for receiving teachings.
All those who have attained the stream-enterer stage possess minds and mental factors capable of cognizing their own intrinsic nature;
yet there are arhats who may be led astray by others.
There is still ignorance,
and there is also hesitation;
it is through the sound of another causing one to awaken that the cause for entering the Path arises.
Suffering can lead one toward the Path;
the discourse on suffering can provide assistance;
and wisdom serves as the preparatory application.
It can extinguish all sufferings and can also bring about happiness;
suffering itself is also nutriment.
One may also dwell for a long time in the eighth stage;
furthermore, it can be said that even those on the stage of nature (gotrabhūmi) are subject to regression.
There is the sense of regression even for a stream-enterer (srotāpanna).
An Arhat has no possibility of falling away;
he possesses neither mundane right view nor the mundane faculty of faith.
There are no indeterminate dharmas.
When entering the state of rightness and departure from birth,
it can be said that all fetters are abandoned.
All those who have attained the stage of stream-entry (srotāpanna) may commit any evil except for the immediate transgressions (ānantarya).
The sūtras spoken by the Buddha are all of definitive meaning (nītārtha).
There are nine kinds of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*):
first, cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*); second, cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
Third, the sphere of infinite space;
fourth, the sphere of infinite consciousness;
fifth, the sphere of nothingness.
Sixth, the sphere of nothingness;
seventh, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
eighth, the nature of the factors of dependent origination.
The nature of the nine factors of the noble path is the mind,
which is intrinsically pure but is said to be impure when it is defiled by adventitious secondary afflictions.
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) are neither mind nor mental factors (caitta),
nor do they have an object of perception (ālambana).
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) are distinct from the outbursts (paryavasthāna), and the outbursts are distinct from the latent dispositions;
it should be stated that the latent dispositions are dissociated from the mind (citta-viprayukta).
The envelopments (paryavasthāna) are associated with the mind.
The past and future do not possess real substantiality.
All dharmas are neither objects of knowledge nor objects of cognition.
It is not something to be fully realized;
there is no intermediate state (antarābhava) at all.
Furthermore, those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna) also attain meditative concentration (dhyāna).
The above are the points of agreement within our own school.
As for the points of divergence among the sub-sects of these four schools,
they concern the various distinctions in the characteristics of each of the Noble Truths as they truly are.
It is so, it is so. There is a distinct realization;
there is a small portion of phenomena that is produced by oneself.
There is some dharma produced by another;
there is some dharma produced by both;
there is some dharma born from a multitude of conditions.
There are times when two minds arise simultaneously;
it is possible for the Path and afflictions to manifest together,
and for karma and its maturation to operate at the same time.
The seed itself becomes the sprout.
The primary elements (mahābhūta) of the material sense faculties possess the sense of transformation;
the mind and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma) do not possess the sense of transformation.
The mind pervades the entire body;
as the mind follows its objects of dependence,
it can be contracted or expanded.
Such various tenets held by these later schools differ from one another in immeasurable ways; however,
the fundamental tenets shared by the Mahīśāsaka school are as follows.
That is to say, the five tones of the Buddha constitute the teaching that transcends the world:
first, impermanence;
second, suffering.
Third, emptiness;
fourth, non-self;
fifth, the tranquility of nirvana.
Because these five can lead one forth to the path of liberation,
whereas the other utterances of the Tathāgata are worldly teachings;
there are arhats who may be led astray by others.
There is still ignorance and there is also hesitation;
it is through the voice of another that one is led to awaken to and enter the Path.
The other schools they adhere to are for the most part the same as the Sarvāstivāda;
their fundamental tenets and doctrines are largely identical to those of the Prajñaptivādins,
namely, that suffering is not the aggregates (*skandha*).
The twelve sense bases are not real;
conditioned phenomena arise through mutual dependence and conjunction,
and are conventionally designated as "suffering."
There is no agency of a person;
there is no untimely death;
it is obtained through prior karma.
With the increase of karma as the cause,
the ripening fruit arises;
through merit, one attains the Noble Path.
The Path cannot be cultivated;
the Path cannot be destroyed.
Other points are for the most part the same as the tenets of the Mahāsāṃghika school.
The Caitīya School, the Aparaśaila School,
and the Uttaraśaila School.
Thus, according to the common tenets of these three schools,
it is said that bodhisattvas do not escape the evil destinies while they are engaged in the practice of making offerings at a stūpa.
One does not attain the great fruit.
There are Arhats who are enticed by others.
These five matters and other thematic gateways [are explained].
Most of what they maintain accords with the teachings of the Mahāsāṃghika school.
Regarding the fundamental tenets shared by the Sarvāstivāda school,
it refers to those things that exist within all [realms] according to the Sarvāstivādins.
All are subsumed under two categories:
one is name (nāma) and the other is form (rūpa).
Furthermore, the substance of the past and future also exists substantially.
All phenomena (dharmas) as bases are objects of knowledge;
they are also objects of cognition and of thorough penetration.
Their characteristics are birth, aging, duration, and impermanence.
They are comprised within the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*).
There are three kinds of conditioned entities (*saṃskṛta-vastu*),
and there are likewise three kinds of unconditioned entities (*asaṃskṛta-vastu*).
The three characteristics of the conditioned possess distinct substantial entities.
Three truths are conditioned;
one truth is unconditioned.
The gradual clear realization of the Four Noble Truths,
based on the two samādhis of emptiness and wishlessness,
both permit entry into the state of rightness and departure from birth.
By contemplating the formations of the desire realm, one enters the state of right determination and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Once one has already entered this state of right determination and departure from birth,
the period of fifteen moments of mind is called "practicing toward" (*pratipannaka*).
The sixteenth moment of mind is designated as "abiding in the fruit.
Regarding the three grades of the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) within a single moment of mind,
the supreme mundane dharma is definitively incapable of retrogression.
For those who have entered the stream (srotāpanna), there is no possibility of falling back;
for Arhats, there is the possibility of falling back.
Not all Arhats attain the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna).
Ordinary worldlings are able to sever sensual desire and ill will;
there are various non-Buddhist practitioners who can attain the five supernormal powers,
and there are also those among the devas who dwell in the holy life.
The factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) are obtainable within seven attainments (samāpatti), but not in the others.
All dhyānas are subsumed under the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna).
Without relying on dhyāna,
one may enter the state of rightness and departure from birth,
and also attain the fruit of arhatship.
If one relies on a body belonging to the form realm or the formless realm,
although one may realize the fruit of arhatship,
one cannot enter the state of right determination and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma).
Based on a body in the desire realm, one is not only able to enter the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*),
but can also realize the fruit of arhatship. However,
in Uttarakuru, there are none who are free from defilement.
The Noble Ones are not born there [in the Formless Realm] nor in the Heaven of Non-perception.
Furthermore, the four fruits of śrāmaṇya are not necessarily attained gradually;
this is the case if one has already entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Based on the mundane path, there is the realization of the fruits of once-returner and non-returner;
it can be said that the four foundations of mindfulness encompass all phenomena.
All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are mental factors (*caitta*).
They are associated with the mind and possess objects of perception (*ālambana*).
All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are subsumed under the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*),
but not all outbursts are subsumed under the latent dispositions.
The nature of the factors of dependent origination is necessarily conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Furthermore, there are factors of dependent origination that continue to function even in an Arhat;
there are Arhats who increase their meritorious karma.
Only in the realms of desire and form does the intermediate state (antarābhava) exist.
The five groups of consciousness, such as the visual consciousness and so forth, may be either defiled or free from defilement;
they grasp only specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) and are exclusively non-conceptual (nirvikalpa).
The entities of the mind and mental factors each exist substantially.
The mind and mental factors necessarily possess objects of perception.
A self-nature does not associate with itself.
The mind does not associate with the mind.
There is mundane right view;
there is the mundane faculty of faith.
There are indeterminate dharmas, and Arhats also possess dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
While all Arhats have attained meditative absorption (dhyāna),
not all are able to bring meditative absorption into manifestation.
There are Arhats who still experience the results of past karma.
There are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who die while abiding in a virtuous state of mind;
however, one in a state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita*) will certainly not pass away.
The liberation of the Buddha and that of the followers of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) are no different;
however, there are distinct differences among the noble paths of the three vehicles.
Furthermore, the Buddha’s equanimity of compassion does not take sentient beings as its object.
Those who cling to the existence of sentient beings do not attain liberation;
one should say that such a bodhisattva is still merely an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
As long as the various fetters have not been severed,
and one has not yet entered the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma),
one is not said to have transcended the stage of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana-bhūmi).
Sentient beings are merely conventionally designated based on the existing continuity of appropriated aggregates.
It is taught that all conditioned phenomena are momentary;
certainly, there is not even the slightest dharma that can transition from a previous life to a subsequent life.
There exists only the conventional person (*pudgala*),
which is said to undergo transmigration;
at the time of death, the aggregate of formations ceases without remainder.
There are non-transformative aggregates;
there is supramundane dhyāna;
and vitarka is also untainted.
That which is wholesome has a cause.
In the state of meditative equipoise, there is no utterance of speech.
The Noble Eightfold Path is the True Wheel of Dharma.
Not all words of the Tathāgata constitute the turning of the wheel of Dharma;
nor is it the case that a single voice of the Buddha can expound all dharmas.
There are also instances where the World-Honored One speaks words that do not accord with the ultimate meaning.
Not all sūtras spoken by the Buddha are of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
The Buddha himself stated that there are sūtras of non-definitive meaning (*neyārtha*).
These are designated as "the primary tenet of identical meaning" and "the secondary tenet of divergent meaning."
Their categories are boundless.
Regarding the fundamental tenets and common doctrines of the Haimavata school,
they maintain that all bodhisattvas are still ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
When the Bodhisattva enters the womb, he does not give rise to craving or attachment.
Among all non-Buddhists, none are able to attain the five supernormal powers,
nor is there anyone among the gods who dwells as a practitioner of the Brahma-faring life.
There are Arhats who, being led astray by others,
still possess ignorance and also harbor doubt.
He causes others to enter into awakening.
The Path arises from sound.
Other points of their tenets are for the most part the same as those of the Sarvāstivādins.
The fundamental tenets of the Vātsīputrīya school are as follows:
the *pudgala* is neither identical to the aggregates (*skandha*) nor distinct from them;
it is a conventional designation (*prajñapti*) based upon the aggregates, bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).
Conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) both abide for a time and perish moment by moment;
this is so whether dharmas are considered apart from a person (pudgala).
There is no transition from a previous life to a subsequent life;
it is only in dependence upon the *pudgala* that one can speak of such a transmigration.
Furthermore, there are non-Buddhists who are able to attain the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
The five consciousnesses are neither defiled nor free from defilement;
if one severs the fetters of the desire realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation,
this is called "freedom from desire."
It is not to be abandoned by insight;

this is the defining characteristic of the "patience" (kṣānti). The "Supreme Mundane Dharmas" (laukikāgradharma) are called "that which leads toward entry into the state of rightness and departure from birth" (samyaktva-niyāma-avakrānti).
If one has already attained entry into the path of rightness and is separated from the state of ordinary birth,
the twelve moments of mind must be called "practicing for the goal" (pratipannaka);
the thirteenth moment of mind is called "abiding in the fruit" (phalastha).
There are many such diverse meanings;
due to differing interpretations of a single verse,
four schools emerged from within this sect.
Namely, the Dharmottarīya,
the Bhadrayānīya,
and the Saṃmitīya schools.
The *Guhyakagiri-vibhāga* explains the verse as follows:
"Having already attained liberation, one falls once again."
Falling away due to craving, one returns; yet,
having attained peace, joy, and what is delightful,
one proceeds according to one's pleasure toward the ultimate bliss.
The fundamental tenets shared by the Mahīśāsaka school are as follows:
the past and the future are non-existent; the present exists;
and unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta) exist.
The four noble truths are realized simultaneously.
When one perceives the truth of suffering, one is able to perceive all the truths;
it is only for one who has already seen them that such a perception is possible.
The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are neither mind nor mental factors,
nor do they enter into anything. Furthermore, "sleeping" (*mīna*) is distinct from the "outbursts" (*paryavasthāna*).
The intrinsic nature of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) is dissociated from the mind;
the intrinsic nature of the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) is associated with the mind.
Ordinary beings do not sever sensual desire or ill will.
There are no non-Buddhists who can attain the five supernormal powers,
nor are there any among the gods who dwell as practitioners of the holy life;
it is certain that there is no intermediate state (antarābhava).
Arhats do not increase meritorious karma.
The five consciousnesses are both associated with defilement and dissociated from defilement.
All six consciousnesses are associated with vitarka and vicāra.
There is also the individual with a shaven head who possesses mundane right view but lacks the mundane faculty of faith.
There is no supramundane dhyāna,
nor are there untainted vitarka and vicāra;
if one who possesses the cause [of such states] were to fall away from the state of a stream-enterer.
All Arhats are certainly free from regression.
The factors of the path are all subsumed within the foundations of mindfulness.
There are nine kinds of unconditioned dharmas.
1. Cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha). 2. Cessation not through deliberation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha). 3. Space (ākāśa).
Fourth, the unconditioned;
fifth, the suchness of wholesome phenomena;
sixth, the suchness of unwholesome phenomena.
7. The suchness of the seven indeterminate phenomena;
8. The suchness of the factors of the path;
9. The suchness of dependent origination.
From conception as the beginning to death as the end,
the material sense faculties and the primary elements all undergo transformation;
likewise, the mind and mental factors also undergo transformation.
The Buddha is within the Sangha;
therefore, one who makes an offering to the Sangha obtains a great fruit,
rather than making a separate offering to the Buddha alone.
The Buddha and those of the two vehicles share the same path and the same liberation.
It is taught that all conditioned phenomena are momentary;
there is certainly not even the slightest dharma that can transition from a previous life to a subsequent one.
These are the points of common doctrine within their own school.
As for the divergent views of their sub-sects,
they maintain that the past and the future exist substantially.
There is also an intermediate state (antarābhava).
All bases of phenomena (dharmāyatana) are objects of knowledge (jñeya) and are also objects of cognition (vijñeya).
Karma is in fact volition (*cetanā*).
There is no physical or vocal karma. It is associated with applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
Even if one performs acts of worship toward a stūpa that has endured for an entire kalpa upon the great earth,
the fruit obtained will be small.

According to the final tenet of this school, the intrinsic nature of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) always abides in the present; likewise, the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) also always abide in the present.
Because there are differing interpretations regarding the meaning of a single verse, as that verse says:
"Five factors are certainly able to bind; from them all sufferings arise."
That is to say: ignorance, craving, the five views, and all karmas.
This is the fundamental tenet shared by the Dharmaguptaka school.
It maintains that although the Buddha is included within the Saṃgha, [he is distinct from it].
However, making a separate offering to the Buddha’s fruit is not the same as offering to the Saṃgha;
by performing acts of worship toward a stūpa, one obtains vast fruits.
Although the liberation of the Buddha and that of the two vehicles is one and the same, [the merit differs].
However, the noble path is distinct;
no non-Buddhists are able to attain the five supernormal powers,
and the bodies of all arhats are entirely untainted (anāsrava).
Other points are for the most part identical to the tenets of the Mahāsāṃghika school.
Regarding the fundamental tenets of the Kāśyapīya school,
they maintain that if a phenomenon has been abandoned and fully understood, it no longer exists.
If it has not been abandoned and not fully understood, it exists;
if the fruit of the karma has already ripened, it does not exist;
if the fruit of the karma has not yet ripened, it exists.
There are conditioned phenomena that have the past as their cause;
there are no conditioned phenomena that have the future as their cause.
All conditioned phenomena perish moment by moment.
All dharmas of those in training (*śaikṣa*) possess a ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*).
Other points are for the most part the same as the tenets of the Dharmaguptaka school.
These are the fundamental tenets and common doctrines of the Sautrāntika school.
This refers to the teaching that the aggregates (skandhas) transition from a previous life to a subsequent life;
the designation "transition" (*saṃkrānti*) is established, yet it does not exist apart from the Noble Path,
for there is the eternal cessation of the aggregates.
There are aggregates at the limit of the faculties,
and there is an aggregate of a single flavor;
even within the state of an ordinary person, there exist noble dharmas.
They maintain that there exists a person (*pudgala*) in the ultimate sense;
in other respects, their tenets are for the most part the same as those of the Sarvāstivādins.
The Tripitaka Dharma Master has finished translating this treatise.
To explain the intent of this retranslation,
he spoke these verses:
Having examined in detail all the various Sanskrit manuscripts, I have retranslated the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* (Treatise on the Wheel of the Doctrine).
The phrasing is elegant, the meaning is flawless, and it should be diligently studied by the wise.
*Treatise on the Doctrinal Differences of the Various Schools*, one fascicle.
